summary: Luke Alvoeiro, who leads core agent harness work at Factory and previously co-created Goose at Block, argues that the bottleneck in software engineering is no longer model intelligence but human attention. He proposes a taxonomy of five frontier multi-agent frameworks: delegation, creator-verifier, direct communication, negotiation, and broadcast. Missions is Factory's answer, composing delegation, creator-verifier, broadcast, and negotiation into a single workflow using a three-role architecture: an orchestrator for planning that produces a validation contract defining 'done' before any coding; workers that implement features with clean context and commit via Git; and validators that perform adversarial verification through scrutiny validators (tests, type checks, lint, code review) and user testing validators (spawning the app, interacting via computer use, checking functional flows end-to-end). Validation contracts are written during planning because tests written after implementation confirm decisions rather than catch bugs. Context preservation relies on structured handoffs documenting completed work, remaining work, commands run, exit codes, issues, and procedural compliance; errors caught at milestone boundaries enable self-healing. Serial execution is chosen over parallel because agents conflict, step on each other's changes, duplicate work, and make inconsistent decisions—coordination overhead negates speed gains while burning tokens. Read-only operations within features and validators are parallelized. Model selection per role is a compounding advantage, and the architecture also compensates for non-frontier models: validation contracts and milestone checkpoints enable successful runs even with open-weight models. Production data from building a Slack clone reveals 60% of time and tokens spent on implementation, validation never succeeding on first attempt, 50% of final lines of code being tests with 90% coverage, and heavy use of prompt caching. To survive the 'bitter lesson' of model releases obsoleting architectures, almost all orchestration logic lives in ~700 lines of prompts and skills rather than a hard-coded state machine; only thin deterministic logic handles bookkeeping like running validation and blocking progress on unresolved handoffs. This means Missions improves with each model generation. The economics shift: a team of five engineers managing 10 work streams can now handle 30, focusing on architecture and product decisions while the codebase ends up cleaner than when started—tests, skills, and structure make agents and humans more productive going forward.

takeaways: The bottleneck in software engineering is human attention, not model intelligence—models can handle full backlogs but humans can only supervise a few tasks at a time.
Missions composes four of five frontier multi-agent frameworks into a three-role architecture: orchestrator (planning), workers (implementation), validators (adversarial verification).
Validation contracts define correctness before implementation; tests written after code confirm decisions rather than catch bugs.
Serial execution with targeted internal parallelization outperforms full parallelism because coordination overhead negates speed gains while burning tokens.
Strategic model selection per role is a structural advantage, and the architecture's validation contracts compensate for non-frontier and open-weight models.
Orchestration logic lives in ~700 lines of prompts and skills, not hard-coded state machines, so the system improves with each model generation rather than being obsoleted.
Production data from a Slack clone: 60% of time/tokens on implementation, 50% of final LOC as tests with 90% coverage, validation never succeeds on first attempt.
Economics shift: a team of five engineers can manage 30 work streams instead of 10, focusing on architecture and product decisions while the codebase ends up cleaner.
Missions has run autonomously for up to 16 days; 30 days is believed possible with the current structure.

sections.title: Introduction: Bottleneck of Human Attention
sections.summary: Luke introduces himself, his background at Block creating Goose and current work at Factory. He claims the bottleneck in software engineering is no longer intelligence but human attention—engineers can only drive a few tasks forward per day despite models being smart enough for all of them.

sections.title: Taxonomy of Five Frontier Multi-Agent Frameworks
sections.summary: Proposes five multi-agent frameworks: delegation (parent spawns child), creator-verifier (separation of concerns for checking), direct communication (agents DM without coordinator), negotiation (coordination over shared resources, ideally positive-sum), and broadcast (one-to-many context sharing for coherence).

sections.title: Missions: Three-Role Architecture
sections.summary: Introduces Missions, combining delegation, creator-verifier, broadcast, and negotiation. Uses orchestrator (planning, validation contract), workers (clean-context implementation, Git commits), and validators (behavioral verification beyond lint and tests). Not a single agent session but an ecosystem communicating through structured handoffs and shared state.

sections.title: Validation Contracts and Adversarial Verification
sections.summary: Explains why validation contracts matter: tests written after implementation confirm decisions, not catch bugs. Contracts are written during planning with hundreds of assertions. Two validator types: scrutiny (tests, lint, type check, code review agents) and user testing (spawns app, interacts via computer use, checks functional flows). Neither validator has seen the code before—validation is adversarial by design. Most wall-clock time is spent on real-world execution, not token generation.

sections.title: Structured Handoffs for Long-Term Context
sections.summary: Workers fill out structured handoffs detailing completed work, unfinished work, commands run, exit codes, issues discovered, and procedural compliance. Errors caught at milestone boundaries trigger scoped corrective work. Longest mission ran 16 days; 30 believed possible. Structure enables long-running autonomy.

sections.title: Serial Execution Over Parallel
sections.summary: Parallelism fails in software dev because agents conflict, step on changes, duplicate work, and make inconsistent decisions. Missions runs features serially—one worker or validator at a time—with parallelization only on read-only operations like codebase search, API research, and code review. Error rate drops dramatically and correctness compounds over multi-day runs.

sections.title: Mission Control: Monitoring Agent Progress
sections.summary: Standard chat interfaces don't suit multi-day tasks. Mission control provides a dedicated view showing project completion, budget consumption, active worker actions, handoff summaries, and validator discoveries. Enables asynchronous oversight as a project manager.

sections.title: Strategic Model Selection Per Role (Droid Whispering)
sections.summary: Planning benefits from slow reasoning, implementation from fast code fluency, validation from precise instruction following. No single model or provider excels at all three. 'Droid whispering' is the skill of modeling how different LLMs interact and fail over multi-day runs. Model-agnostic architecture is a structural advantage—you're only as strong as your weakest link if locked into one provider.

sections.title: Production Data: Building a Slack Clone
sections.summary: Walks through a real Slack clone build. 60% of time and tokens go to implementation. Validation never succeeds on first attempt, demonstrating the value of the QA loop with follow-up features. 50% of final lines of code are tests with 90% coverage. Heavy prompt caching offsets the cost of long-running tasks. Enterprise use cases include overnight prototyping, internal tooling, huge refactors and migrations, ML search research, and codebase modernization for better agent productivity.

sections.title: Designing Systems That Improve With Each Model Generation
sections.summary: Addresses the 'bitter lesson' fear that new model releases obsolete custom architectures. Missions was designed to improve with every model improvement: almost all orchestration logic lives in ~700 lines of prompts and skills, not a hard-coded state machine. Four sentences can alter execution strategy dramatically. Worker behavior is driven by per-mission skills the orchestrator defines. Only thin deterministic logic handles bookkeeping—running validation, blocking progress on unresolved handoffs. Missions ensure discipline; models provide intelligence via familiar primitives like agents.md and skills. Structure also compensates for non-frontier and open-weight models.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Shifting Economics of Software Engineering
sections.summary: The economics are changing: a team of five engineers managing 10 work streams can now handle 30, focusing on architecture and product decisions instead of execution. The codebase ends up cleaner than when started—tests, skills, and structure make agents and humans more productive going forward. Recaps how the four strategies compose: delegation in orchestrator spawning, creator-verifier in separated validation, broadcast in shared mission state, negotiation at milestone boundaries. Strategies alone aren't enough; structured handoffs, per-role model selection, and model-improving architecture are the connective tissue. Open questions remain about further parallelization and orchestrating missions into more complex workflows. Closes with a call to try /missions in Open Droid.
